text.p: The future cost of state funding of pensions in Europe will jeopardise efforts to sustain the European Union's three percent budget deficit target for several decades in many EU states, industry members said on Friday.
They told a fund management conference the funding crisis would directly threaten monetary stability and the future success of the single currency.
The only way to ensure adequate pension provision and maintain stability was through funded schemes.

"There is too heavy a reliance on Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG) financing now throughout the EU. About 85 percent of the total macro-economic pension pay-out is PAYG financed," said Koen de Ryck, permanent representative of the European Federation for Retirement Provision.

He said EU pension fund assets totalled about $1.5 trillion at the end of 1995 -- representing only a third of U.S. assets despite the U.S. having some 100 million fewer people than the EU. Moreover, only two countries, the UK and the Netherlands, make up 74 percent of those EU pension fund assets.
By 2020, he estimated EU pension fund assets would still total only half those of the U.S. despite extended coverage and the expected shift towards funding of pensions.
"The EU may reach $15 trillion pension fund assets in 2020 (growing at nine percent a year), but the U.S. (also at nine percent a year) would have $37.9 trillion."
De Ryck said the shortfall of contributions to payments in EU countries was considerable at between 10 and 30 percent of total security pensions payout, with Italy regarded as the worst case.

"The shortfall is subsidised and that worsens public deficits...To sustain current or even lower benefits, future generations will have to bear a much higher burden in terms of contributions and taxation," he said.
Adam Lessing, managing director of Creditanstalt mutual fund group OIG, said the unfunded pension liabilities of the state PAYG systems were estimated at over $14 trillion.
Without a move to funding, and given the trend of a growing retirement population, rising deficits would be unsustainable.
Lessing said it was clear that the total funding of Europe's pension liabilities was not an option and that partial funding would take time, but it represented a major opportunity for the industry.

Herbert Wunderlicht, managing director of Dresdner Capital International, said PAYG schemes were too expensive and held major future risks. A move to private pension provision, and specifically defined contribution, would ease the state burden.
"The role of the state has to diminish as costs are spiralling out of control."
He said the greatest opportunity for the industry lay in the countries with the lowest levels of pension fund assets relative to GDP such as France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Austria and Belgium.

He said he expected defined contribution plans over the next few years to constitute a significant part of the European pensions market, and saw big local banks and insurance companies dominating due to brand recognition and distribution resources.
He estimated there would be another $400 billion in European defined contribution assets by 2000.
